meta.title: Yoruba A1 Beginner
meta.subtitle: 500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Yoruba → English (see the Yoruba, recall the meaning) and English → Yoruba (see an English meaning, recall the Yoruba). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 500 words for a beginner, aligned to A1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand and use familiar everyday expressions and very basic phrases aimed at the satisfaction of needs of a concrete type' — a learner here is able to introduce themselves and others, to ask and answer questions about personal details such as where they live, people they know and things they have, and to interact in a simple way provided the other person talks slowly and clearly and is prepared to help. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for Yoruba, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 321 of the 500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — greetings and politeness, the pronouns, question and joining words, numbers, people and the family, the body and feeling ill, time and the days of the week, food and drink, money and shopping, the home and clothes, the town and getting about, the weather, colours, animals, school and work, the everyday verbs, describing things, and the little words of place and manner every sentence is built out of — and the other 179 are the commonest remaining words of the Yoruba Wikipedia (its articles of 150 words or more, the one-line stubs left out). About half of that Wikipedia is written with its tone marks, and the counts of the carefully marked articles decide how an unmarked spelling is shared out among the words it could be (ti, tí, tì). The corpus is encyclopaedic, which shows in the fill (government, history, sport), and the cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words met most often come first. Only words English Wiktionary has an entry for can be taught here, and some of the commonest are missing from it (ta ni 'who', ibo 'where', nísinsìnyí 'now', tún 'again', burú 'to be bad'). Every word is written in standard Yoruba spelling WITH ITS TONE MARKS — an acute for a high tone (á), a grave for a low one (à), no mark for a mid tone — because the tones are part of the word: ọkọ is 'husband', ọkọ̀ 'vehicle', ọkọ́ 'hoe'. The Alphabet deck, first in this collection, teaches the letters and the marks. One spelling is often several words (dá 'to create', 'to stop', 'to break'); the card is the spelling and gives the first meaning of each. Many Yoruba adjectives are verbs ('to be big', 'to be good'), and are taught as Wiktionary gives them. Example sentences are few: 182 of the 500 words have one, from Wiktionary's usage examples and from Tatoeba, which holds about 60 Yoruba sentences with a translation; none is invented. There is no speaker button: few devices have a Yoruba voice, and one without it would read the word in another language's sounds. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, spellings and tone marks: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: the Yoruba Wikipedia, articles of the 2026-11-01 dump (CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: English Wiktionary (CC BY-SA 4.0) and Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
